POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 14:49:19 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Russian strikes leave thousands without power in Ukraine, says Zelenskyy https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-strikes-leave-thousands-without-power-ukraine-volodymyr-zelenskyy/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 01 Nov 2026 14:48:54 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9251463 Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure have left thousands of households without electricity, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

“Overnight alone, our energy infrastructure came under Russian attack in four regions: Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, and Khmelnytskyi. Substations, transformers, and power lines that supply electricity to our people’s homes were targeted, Zelenskyy wrote on social media. 

“As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without power,” he added, noting that the “intensity of the strikes is extremely high.”

Zelenskyy’s comments came as Russian authorities reported a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike overnight on an industrial facility in the Nizhny Novgorod region.

“A massive drone attack occurred overnight and this morning in the Nizhny Novgorod region: more than a hundred drones were destroyed,” Gleb Nikitin, the region’s governor, wrote on Telegram on Sunday.

“According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties,” he said, adding that an industrial facility in the Kstovsky district sustained “significant damage.”

“During the restoration process, temporary power outages and reduced hot water and heating services are possible in certain sections of the utility networks supplying residential buildings,” he wrote.

Nikitin did not specify which industrial facility had been attacked. The NORSI oil refinery is located in the region.

On Friday, the local governor of Russia’s Samara region blamed Ukraine for an early morning drone attack that struck an oil refinery in Novokuibyshevsk city.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Kyiv agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ukraine paused drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for 72 hours when Trump announced an energy ceasefire in October, but the Kremlin continued to bombard Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

]]> en Commission backs Tusk as he vows no compromise in court showdown https://www.politico.eu/article/european-commission-backs-donald-tusk-over-poland-constitutional-court-judges/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:52:15 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9251052 The European Commission has reiterated that Poland’s parliament must have the right to appoint new judges, lending support to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in an escalating confrontation over the country’s Constitutional Tribunal.

The dispute pits Tusk’s government against President Karol Nawrocki over efforts to reverse judicial changes introduced by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2015 and 2023, which drew condemnation from European courts over concerns about judicial independence.

Nawrocki, elected with PiS backing in 2025, has refused to swear in some Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority, while the court’s PiS-linked leadership has prevented them from working.

The Commission said it was closely monitoring developments and, in a carefully worded statement to POLITICO, appeared to show support for Tusk’s position.

“The Polish Constitutional Tribunal needs to be able to function in accordance with the Polish constitution and the case law of the Court of Justice of the EU,” Commissioner for Democracy, Justice and the Rule of Law Michael McGrath said.

“This matters for every Polish citizen, and it is for the Polish authorities to ensure that,” McGrath added, stating that “the Venice Commission has been clear that appointing the new judges lies within the power of the Sejm [Poland’s lower house of parliament].”

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk vowed Saturday night not to back down on the dispute. “In some matters there can be no compromise,” Tusk said in an address to the nation, comparing calls for reconciliation to a thief demanding to keep half the contents of a stolen handbag.

“We have waited too long for the treasure of an independent, democratic Poland to be frightened into retreat,” Tusk said.

The prime minister also targeted Nawrocki, who turned his plane around mid-flight en route to Senegal and returned to Warsaw, where he pushed his way into the Tribunal shortly after midnight Saturday, confronting judges challenging its leadership.

“In a state governed by the rule of law, a politician cannot enter a court or tribunal and give orders or intimidate judges, even if he is the president,” Tusk said.

He pledged to ensure the Tribunal could operate independently and safely.

In his statement to POLITICO, McGrath stopped short of endorsing Friday’s suspension of Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański, a move that triggered the latest spat.

Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, taking charge of the Tribunal, suspended Święczkowski and Sochański after they blocked judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority from work for months. 

Nawrocki denounced the move as an unlawful takeover and held talks with parliamentary leaders Saturday, boycotted by Tusk’s Civic Coalition and its government ally, the New Left.

Korwin-Piotrowska has convened an assembly of Tribunal judges for Tuesday, potentially setting up another confrontation over who controls the court.

Gerardo Fortuna contributed to this report.

]]> en UK’s future lies in EU, says Rachel Reeves https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-future-eu-says-rachel-reeves/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:45:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9250989 Former British chancellor Rachel Reeves has stated that the U.K.’s future should be in the European Union, arguing Brexit has been bad for Britain.

Writing in the Sunday Times, Reeves, who was sacked as chancellor by Prime Minister Andy Burnham when he entered Downing Street, said: “I am proud of the progress we have already made in strengthening our relationship with the European Union. Brexit has made us poorer, weaker and less secure.

“There is a debate to be had about our future relationship with Europe, and I welcome Andy Burnham’s leadership in facing up to this. No one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were.”

Reeves added that while she believes “Britain’s future lies in the European Union”, it was “incumbent on supporters of our re-entry to make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right.”

Last week, Burnham expressed an openness to restarting free movement between the U.K and the EU. He also said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament.

At the last election, Labour’s manifesto — which Reeves helped to draw up — said a Labour government would stay outside the EU.

But at the Labour Party’s conference in September, Burnham called for closer links with the bloc.

Reeves’ intervention comes ahead of a leaders’ summit later this month where she said “at a minimum” she hoped to see confirmation of a youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for.

At the Nov. 20 summit, the EU and the U.K. hope to sign off on a set of agreements ranging from trade to climate regulations.

]]> en How Merz’s five-day Asia trip ended up being mostly about Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/friedrich-merz-asia-trip-europe-security-cooperation/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 01 Nov 2026 09:07:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9250152 KOREAN DEMILITARIZED ZONE — Friedrich Merz ended his five-day trip to Asia on Friday reflecting on Europe’s past.

After visiting the blue barracks where the armistice that ended the Korean War was signed in 1953, in the Joint Security Area where North and South Korean troops stand face-to-face, the German chancellor addressed the obvious parallels between his country’s history and Korea’s present.

“Thoughts are running through my mind about how grateful we may be that in Germany we haven’t had to experience this for 36 years,” Merz said.

The remarks concluded a tour of Singapore, Japan and South Korea, where the chancellor was challenged by Asian capitals over security and trade cooperation — and often reminded of how the region’s turmoil are intertwined with Europe’s precarious moment.

‘Collective security’

One only has to look across the border. Shortly before Merz arrived in the demilitarized zone, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan. The chancellor’s greatest security concerns at home — Russia’s war against Ukraine and Moscow’s threat to Europe — are increasingly becoming problems in the Asia-Pacific region as well.

The fact that Pyongyang is able to launch so many ballistic missiles, testing and expanding its long-range strike capabilities, is directly linked to its cooperation with Russia. North Korea has been sending soldiers to the Russian front in Ukraine for two years and in return benefited from combat experience and technology transfers.

North Korean state television on Thursday showed leader Kim Jong Un with new military drones, including a potential stealth drone, underscoring the great strides the country is also making in drone development. These are serious security issues that other countries in the region, including Japan, cannot ignore.

Besides provocations from Pyongyang, there is China, which is not only becoming increasingly dominant in trade but also casting its eye toward Taiwan, making far-reaching territorial claims in the South China Sea and putting strong pressure on critics such as Japan. And there is Russia, which is forging close military ties with Beijing and carrying out joint bomber flights with the Chinese air force near the Japanese border.

“Russia’s war against Ukraine is ever-present here in the region,” Merz told reporters following his visit to the border. “There is no longer such a thing as unilateral security in the world, only collective security,” he added, underscoring his call to “work closely” with Japan, South Korea and Singapore “on security policy issues” and in the defense industry.

Middle power struggle

This German offer has generated considerable interest. Given Berlin’s position as Ukraine’s largest supporter, German defense companies are highly active in the war-torn country and cooperate with local manufacturers, giving them access to rapid technological developments. This makes them attractive to Asian partners who fear falling behind North Korea and China as they benefit from their cooperation with Russia.

The fact that the chancellor traveled with a large business delegation — the kind previously seen only on visits to China — underscores this focus. Among the companies were several defense firms, including aircraft manufacturer Airbus, air defense manufacturer Diehl Defense and drone specialist Quantum-Systems. Japan welcomed the cooperation, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaking of a “premium partnership” with Germany.

Yet Merz’s trip was about more than defense deals. The chancellor used his visits to warn against violations of international law by Russia but also increasingly by China and the United States. “We are on the threshold of a new era,” he said in Tokyo. “We are witnessing how the major powers are pursuing a new policy and how international rules are eroding.”

His words echoed a similar warning issued by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier during a parallel trip to Beijing. “An order that was never perfect, but at least served as the foundation for international cooperation, is eroding. Lawlessness looms. I see this as a great danger for all of us,” said Steinmeier.

To counter this trend, Merz built on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposal that “middle powers” should team up to better defend themselves in the face of unreliable major powers and toothless international organizations.

In speeches in Tokyo and Seoul, Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade.” Medium-sized powers such as the EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted,” said the chancellor.

It’s a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals and the tariff threats made by U.S. President Donald Trump. Merz also said the alliance could strengthen the World Trade Organization and seek to unblock the nomination of judges to the organization’s appellate body.

“Considerable concern” over Franco-German car deal

During his trip, however, Merz experienced firsthand just how difficult it is to put such an ambitious proposal into practice when special interests complicate an alliance of small and medium-sized powers.

This became most evident when the Asian countries issued a sharp protest over planned “Made in Europe” rules for the car industry. Under a proposal agreed by Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, Brussels would restrict subsidies for cars to vehicles produced inside the EU, Switzerland and the U.K., putting foreign manufacturers at a disadvantage.

In polite but direct terms, South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung told reporters he had “asked Merz for support so that Korea would be treated like the EU member states.” A similar complaint was voiced in Japan.

“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning to Germany on Friday evening. He admitted that the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”

Merz vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and raise them at the next EU leaders’ summit. Yet they are a sharp reminder of how much industry-specific details can hamper the implementation of his proposed broader alliance.

The chancellor’s trip also revealed challenges when it comes to security cooperation: A request for Japan to supply Patriot anti-aircraft missiles to Ukraine fell flat. And it remains unclear whether Tokyo continues to contribute several billions to a new Ukraine loan next year, as Brussels hopes.

A Japanese diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, posed a different question to the German delegation: “How exactly will you help us if China attacks Taiwan?”

Deutschland befindet sich nicht im Krieg, aber auch nicht mehr im Frieden. Was passiert konkret, wenn das Land militärisch angegriffen wird? Ein konventioneller Überraschungsangriff gilt dank engmaschiger Überwachung als unwahrscheinlich, doch der hybride Schattenkrieg durch Sabotage und Spionage läuft bereits auf Hochtouren. ]]> de Hundreds of thousands of protesters march across France for third week in a row https://www.politico.eu/article/france-youth-protests-cost-of-living-spread-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 17:33:31 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9250764 Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in France to protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating school conditions as youth-led protests spread to Italy and Germany.

With six months to go until the presidential election, France’s largest cities including Paris, Lyon and Marseille saw marches for a third consecutive Saturday.

The French interior ministry said 320,000 people took to the streets across the country on Saturday in what were largely peaceful protests. Student unions put the figure at half a million, including 200,000 in Paris.

Arrests were significantly lower than during previous demonstrations, although tensions and clashes emerged in Marseille, Paris and Lyon as marches dispersed.

French authorities described the situation nationwide as “generally calm” in the early afternoon. France deployed 70,000 police officers to contain what it feared would be another day of unrest.

Many protesters wore Halloween costumes despite French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warning that face coverings could result in fines of €150.

Other European cities including Rome, Milan, Berlin and Frankfurt also experienced a day of youth-led protests against the cost of living and, in Germany, military spending.

The protests in over 30 German cities were ignited by a youth-led initiative called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z gets things done) and remained largely peaceful despite the police cancelling a planned march in Cologne after some participants wore face coverings and set off smoke bombs.

In Italy, the police carried out 60 searches across 23 cities targeting people suspected of inciting violence a mass demonstrations on Friday, according to news agency ANSA.

]]> en Putin’s potential G20 comeback risks normalizing Russian war crimes, says Kallas https://www.politico.eu/article/kaja-kallas-vladimir-putin-g20-return-risks-normalizing-russian-war-crimes/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 16:41:12 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9250641 Vladimir Putin’s possible return to a G20 summit in Florida in December risks normalizing Russia’s war crimes in Ukraine, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Saturday.

“Normalizing Russia coming back to these international fora is just normalizing war crimes being committed every day now” in Ukraine, Kallas said in an interview with Bloomberg TV.

She added that Russia’s war in Ukraine conflicts “with U.N charter principles that all these countries around the table have signed up to.”

Putin hasn’t yet confirmed whether he would attend the December summit hosted in the U.S. His last in-person attendance at a G20 meeting was in 2019 — three years before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kallas’ remarks come amid growing frustration among EU countries over Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov’s attendance at a G20 ministerial gathering in Atlanta.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was hosting the meeting, called off the traditional family photo after European officials refused to stand beside Lavrov.

Kallas said in the interview that “we don’t want to stand next to him [Lavrov] in this fora,” because he’s been placed under international sanctions.

However, she added that Lavrov’s presence meant “we can also immediately fight back on these lies” from Russia.

Kallas hailed the U.S. decision on Friday to sell 500 Patriot missile interceptors to Ukraine as a “very positive development” and called on allies to toughen sanctions against Russia.

A former Prime Minister of Estonia, Kallas has emerged as one of the EU’s most vocal critics of Russia.

In the interview, she rebuffed reported calls from the Pentagon for NATO countries, including the Baltic states that border Russia, to tone down their criticism of the Kremlin.

“The question is if you don’t talk about the threat, is it going away? I think it’s not going away.”

]]> en Burnham ‘open’ to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-open-to-formal-apology-for-britain-slave-trade/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:55:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9250317 U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was “open” to calls for the British state to formally apologize for its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

Burnham offered a “structured dialogue with those affected” by the slave trade in an opinion piece for the Guardian, published ahead of a summit of Commonwealth countries starting Sunday.

“Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do,” Burnham wrote.

However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay financial reparations for the slave trade, saying that they would be the wrong solution.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” the prime minister argued.

Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced in June a manifesto by Caribbean leaders setting out the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations from former colonial powers.

Burnham will attend the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, which runs through Wednesday. It will be his first foreign trip with King Charles.

It will be a crucial test for the prime minister, who will try to avoid a fight over slavery reparations that marred his predecessor Keir Starmer’s visit at the last summit in 2024.

]]> en Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymyr-zelenskyy-urges-us-speed-up-patriot-deliveries/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:41:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9250149 Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for approving the sale of Patriot interceptors but urged Washington to fast-track the delivery of the defensive missiles.

Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision” by the U.S. to approve the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missiles — but said the years-long wait to deliver them was too long for Ukraine’s urgent needs.

“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote in a Facebook post on Friday night.

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.

Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.

In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

“Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said.

The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months.

However, the White House said that it won’t pay for the Patriot interceptors. “The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies,” a statement from the State Department said.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sat, 31 Oct 2026 01:09:52 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 [Interview] Young Europeans know far more about Palestine than young Israelis, says MEP Lucia Yar after West Bank trip https://euobserver.com/245372/interview-young-europeans-know-far-more-about-palestine-than-young-israelis-says-mep-lucia-yar-after-west-bank-trip/ Sun, 01 Nov 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245372 Slovak MEP Lucia Yar reflects on her NGO-led trip to the Middle East: 'When I walk through the streets of Brussels, I see more Palestinian flags than I saw during my entire stay in the West Bank, where the Palestinian flag is perceived as a provocation']]> First published in Respekt.

Slovak Renew Europe MEP Lucia Yar is one of the few MEPs that have travelled to the West Bank and the first Slovak politician to do so since 7 October 2023.

“When I walk through the streets of Brussels, I see more Palestinian flags than I saw during my entire stay in the West Bank,” she said.

In the following interview, Yar discusses her trip to the West Bank and the EU’s scope to influence events in the Middle East.

What stayed with you the most from the trip?

Young people’s feelings. I met a 23-year-old woman who told me that in recent years they had kept no pictures, memorabilia or even a flag at home — nothing that might in any way express her Palestinian identity. She said IDF soldiers had come to their home once and taken away her brother.

Almost every young man in the West Bank has apparently had a similar experience of either being interrogated or detained. When I walk through the streets of Brussels, I see more Palestinian flags than I saw during my entire stay in the West Bank, where the Palestinian flag is perceived as a provocation.

Young people there live under constant surveillance of some kind. In the town where they were born, they have to carry a residence permit card. They live in fear and know nothing else.

I was also struck by the feelings of young people on the Israeli side, who have never spoken to Palestinians and feel only anger. It is an intergenerational trauma on both sides and remains unresolved, affecting millions of people across generations.

Why did you go to the West Bank in the first place? And why now?

The EU or its parliament are yet to obtain permission to organise an official mission. Either it was not possible to agree with the Israeli authorities, or such a mission was blocked within the EP itself. I do not know why it was not possible.

I was invited by DanChurchAid, a humanitarian NGO with roots in the Danish Lutheran Church, active in Israel and the Palestinian territories. Its work is therefore not limited to providing humanitarian aid, but also includes advocacy for not only Christian Palestinians.

As an agnostic, it seemed right for me to go with them, because they offered a balanced programme. Having read a whole lot about the issue and region over a long period and during my studies, I wanted to form my own view through personal experience. It is better to see something once than hear about it a thousand times. And given no Slovak politician had visited the West Bank since October 2023, it was good for someone to go.

How did people react to your trip to the West Bank?

I encountered a full range of reactions online, including some very harsh ones. Strongly pro-Israel comments claimed that by speaking to Palestinians, I was supporting Hamas. Meanwhile, from the far end of the pro-Palestinian side, I heard that this was some kind of performance on my part. In-person reactions were more positive and came from across the political spectrum.

Do you think pro-Palestinian criticism was justified?

In this case, we would not need to comment on events in other parts of the world. I believe the European Parliament is vocal enough on foreign policy. Recently, we dealt with China; before that, the United States; and Ukraine is constantly on our agenda. As the strong democratic voice of all Europeans, the parliament must draw firm attention to certain issues.

Immediately after returning from the West Bank, I spoke about this issue in plenary, and I discussed it personally with Kaja Kallas, the EU foreign affairs chief.

We spoke about why the European Commission has not yet presented a way to sanction a broader group of Israelis operating in illegal settlements or how to apply such sanctions. Some member states have already taken certain steps in this direction.

Read more

Caretaker PM Netanyahu expected to escalate violence, as EU sanctions talk on hold until new Israeli government formed

Other member states may block such sanctions. The EU must decide unanimously on matters of foreign policy.

Suspending the entire association agreement with Israel is unrealistic, but restrictions on trade with Israeli settlers would be different.

Not only does the EU cooperate with settlers, but pension funds in the Netherlands and Sweden invest in businesses operating in these illegal settlements in the West Bank. This is precisely what the commission has the power to limit: it can prepare a relevant proposal and approve it by qualified majority.

In such a case, it would not be possible to block the decision merely by forming a blocking minority. We can press the commission, ask it questions and exert pressure on it. The point is to draw attention to areas where the commission should act. Citizens and MEPs are calling for it. If the proposals ultimately fail, so be it. But we have certain powers, and we should use them.

Why does the commission not want to put forward the options you mentioned, which could be adopted by qualified majority?

We can only speculate about who may be blocking something, whether anyone is blocking it at all, and what forces are at play. We sent the commission a letter asking about these matters as well, but have not received a reply.

You had an opportunity to spend some time in Israel itself. Whom were you able to meet?

We met Israeli politicians who belonged to the opposition but were not enthusiastic about the idea of an independent Palestinian state. We also spoke to representatives of an organisation that helps both Palestinian and Israeli women.

]]> Sovereign AI, male-dominated by design: how EU procurement ignores women-led tech https://euobserver.com/245535/sovereign-ai-male-dominated-by-design-how-eu-procurement-ignores-women-led-tech/ Sun, 01 Nov 2026 07:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245535 Women face greater exposure to AI taking over their tasks, are less represented among the people who build the systems, and are under-financed as founders.]]> In high-income countries, 9.6 percent of employed women work in jobs in the highest exposure category for generative artificial intelligence (AI), against 3.5 percent of men.

Women make up 19.5 percent of information and communication technology specialists in the EU. Start-ups with at least one woman founder receive 12 percent of venture capital.

Women face greater exposure to AI taking over their tasks, are less represented among the people who build the systems, and are under-financed as founders.

Our task force within the Connecting Women in Digital Forum asked a narrow question: where does AI policy risk leaving women out, and which instruments already in motion could change that?

We found five gaps

Nobody has defined a good AI job. The EUCommission could do so, across wages, security, autonomy, progression and voice, in the Quality Jobs Act due later this year.

Member states also have until 2 December to transpose the Platform Work Directive, whose safeguards on algorithmic management are a ready model they can choose to extend beyond platform work.

Transition support follows territories, while AI exposure follows tasks. An administrative worker in a region with no designated just transition territory gets nothing. The next EU budget could make occupational exposure an eligibility trigger, with recipients reported by sex.

European support for women founders stops at a €75,000 grant. Nothing covers the step from there to €2m. The Commission’s Startup and Scaleup Strategy does not even name that gap; the only one it acknowledges sits above €100m. The Action Plan for women in research, innovation and start-ups, still to be adopted, should include a dedicated facility.

Digital Decade reporting counts adoption, not who benefits. Every AI indicator should be paired with a result reported by sex, starting with the December revision of the national roadmaps.

The fifth gap is procurement and it sits at the centre of a debate the EU is already having.

Read more

Revealed: New data shows Big Tech lobbying pushing EU towards sweeping data-protection rollback

Europe’s conversation about technological sovereignty usually begins with infrastructure: compute, chips, cloud and data centres. Sovereignty is also produced through purchasing: public contracts decide which suppliers gain revenue, references, scale and credibility.

In concentrated AI and cloud markets, one significant public contract is often what qualifies a firm to compete for the next.

Public procurement accounts for around 14 percent of EU gross domestic product. The commission’s proposal for a Public Procurement Act, tabled on 9 September, treats that spending explicitly as strategy: simpler rules, but also environmental, social, innovation, security and resilience considerations, and a European preference.

It tracks awards to small and medium-sized enterprises, but it does not track awards to women-led firms.

Start counting the women

The Cloud and AI Development Act, tabled in June, repeats the pattern: Article 33 requires member states to monitor cloud and AI procurement for barriers facing smaller firms and to report annually on their share of contracts, but it says nothing about gender.

Adding women-led firms to that reporting requirement would begin to show who is actually winning Europe’s cloud and AI business.

Procurement data is not currently broken down by technology category or supplier ownership, so policymakers can count contract value without knowing who got the opportunity.

In one version of sovereignty, Europe could spend more public money on AI and end up reinforcing a concentrated supplier market. In another version, public demand could deliberately broaden the range of firms that can build and scale technology in Europe.

Both count as European procurement in the statistics, yet they do not produce the same market.

Importantly, no one needs to wait for the new Act. Article 67  permits contracting authorities to use award criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract, while Article 70 allows conditions governing contract performance. That means a contracting authority can, for example, assess the inclusiveness of the team delivering a contract, where that criterion is sufficiently linked to the contract itself, or require prime contractors to report the share of subcontracted value going to women-led firms.

Spain has legislated equality criteria across every phase of procurement in its science system, and the European Institute for Gender Equality publishes a methodology. The new Act should add a duty to report awards to women-led firms by number and value, so policymakers can see whether those options are actually being used.

AI does not need a separate equality regime.

Each gap we identified can be addressed through an instrument already in force or on the table.

What is missing is not another framework, but action and political will power. So our ask to EU institutions, and to the governments now transposing, budgeting and negotiating these files, is simple: pick one of the five gaps, name the instrument that can close it, and name who in your institution can act on it immediately.

]]> [Interview] Canadian scholar Henry Giroux on ‘gangster capitalism’ and why he supports Europe’s student revolts https://euobserver.com/245348/interview-canadian-scholar-henry-giroux-on-why-europes-student-protests-are-a-revolt-against-gangster-capitalism/ Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245348 Dr Henry Giroux has watched student revolts in Europe and is cheering them on. The scholar of critical pedagogy says ‘gangster capitalism’ is allowing the far-right to thrive and that culture is threatening democracy itself.]]> Across Europe, young people have taken to the streets to demand improved education and voice frustration at generational and structural inequalities.

From Canada, Dr Henry Giroux has watched protests unfold and is cheering them on. Speaking with EUobserver, the scholar of critical pedagogy analyses the root causes of mass discontent. He discussed the global fight for democracy and warns ‘gangster capitalism’ has enabled the far-right to thrive.

You gave a speech in which you said widening inequalities are hollowing out democracy, as well as rising authoritarianism and assaults on public institutions. At what point does a society stop being a democracy?

I think a democracy dies when you no longer have the apparatuses available to take seriously the fact that you can’t have a democracy without informed citizens.

You start seeing inequality translate itself into the criminalisation of culture itself: not simply an attempt to spread ideologies that depoliticise people, but ideologies that are geared at creating a fascist subject – somebody who’s unthinking, doesn’t really understand context or the problems their lives are basically engaged in. Such a person turns to educational institutions – what I call pedagogical regimes of terror – and to communities of hate and bigotry.

Read more

One-in-three European voters now support an authoritarian or populist party, new research reveals

But where the left has really failed around this question is that education is central to politics – it’s not just about schooling, it’s embedded. The most powerful educational institutions today are cultural apparatuses like podcasts, X, or other social media. These are powerful regimes for telling stories that normalise inequality, attack the welfare state, unions, and all those things that make a democracy viable.

When I talk about democracy and education, I don’t ask: ‘What is good educational policy?’. I think the real question is: ‘What kind of education does a democracy require?’

It’s a conversation about power. Who controls the apparatuses of education? What kind of agents are they trying to create? What kind of values are they justifying?

All we have to do is look at what’s happening all over Europe, with respect to these student revolts. There are differences in these revolts, but the overarching connection is that young people are saying, ‘We’ve had enough of gangster capitalism. It’s destroying our lives.’

You can’t have a democracy when it goes after the welfare state. I listen to the French leaders saying things like, ‘Oh, the debt is terrible now. It’s off the charts.’ Well, you know what isn’t off the charts? The growth of money concentrated in the hands of relatively few people. And at the same time, it’s off the charts at the expense of the welfare of students, and others struggling to pay their bills. 

Read more

French school protests to continue, after prime minister ignores demands

You often use the term ‘gangster capitalism’, which is quite strong. Can you define it?

Gangster capitalism concentrates wealth in relatively few hands at the expense of any institution that would make democracy possible because it’s more concerned about the belief in the ability of markets to solve all problems. And it seems to me that it does a few things that we need to talk about.

]]> No extra funds for biodiversity at UN meeting, as vast majority of EU natural treasures left unprotected https://euobserver.com/246078/no-extra-funds-for-biodiversity-at-un-meeting-as-vast-majority-of-eu-natural-treasures-left-unprotected/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:03:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246078 Spending on repairing damaged ecosystems would need to rise fourfould, to almost $300bn to meet the natural protection goal countries set in 2022, a recent UN report found.]]> Spending on repairing damaged ecosystems would need to rise fourfold to almost $300bn (€269m) to meet the natural protection goal which UN countries set in 2022, a new report has found.

Some 250m hectares of natural ecosystems, or an area the size of Kazakhstan, is currently under protection to let it regenerate, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) study.

Presented at the biodiversity conference in Yerevan on Thursday (29 October), the authors said the result was “encouraging,” though it still amounted to only 34 percent of the goal environment ministers from across the world had set themselves for 2030.

At sea and in freshwater ecosystems, the situation was very different, with only 11m hectares protected.

Read more

Europe can’t lead on nature at COP17 while cutting biodiversity cash at home

Protecting natural areas degraded by human activity, such as pollution or overfishing, is key to preserving local species and biodiversity.

UNEP says restoring even 15 percent of priority areas would mean six in 10 species projected to go extinct could be spared.

And while nature restoration is key for food and water security, it is also important for climate resilience, the European Environment Agency (EEA) spokesperson told EUobserver.

The UN agency’s report is the first to gather data for land and water environments and evaluate progress in biodiversity conservation targets there, just as two weeks of negotiations at the biannual ‘COP 17’ meeting close on Friday.

Read more

‘Cementing over our own future’: Europe’s nature loss is 600 football pitches daily

We are “still not restoring nature at the scale or speed required,” said Inger Andersen, UNEP’s executive director, in a statement, urging countries to step up their efforts by the 2030 deadline.

The summit is to conclude with plans for the next four years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway, but significant financial commitments remain unlikely.

Jutta Paulus, a German Greens MEP representing the European Parliament at the conference, said “chronic underfunding” of biodiversity protection is the “main obstacle on our way to food security, a functioning economy and prosperity.”

In terms of ocean restoration, the EU needs “significantly greater investment in restoration, monitoring, and enforcement” to ensure real effects, saaid Nicolas Fournier, campaign director at Oceana in Europe, a marine protection NGO.

“Restoring an area with public money only to allow destructive activities to continue is not restoration – it is a waste of public resources,” he told EUobserver.

In the EU, protected areas amounted to 26 percent of land in 2024, and less than 14 percent of the sea area in 2023, according to EEA data.

To reach the 30 percent target by 2030, member states have to develop national plans, reviewed by the commission and the EEA.

]]> Belgian parliament to vote on divisive new law allowing police raids on people’s homes, if they are suspected of harbouring an undocumented migrant https://euobserver.com/246021/belgian-parliament-to-vote-on-divisive-new-law-allowing-police-raids-on-peoples-homes-if-they-are-suspected-of-harbouring-an-undocumented-migrant/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:45:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246021 “The Belgian government may call them ‘home visits’, but that doesn’t change what they are: police forcibly entering private homes and traumatising families and children to arrest people", said one critic of the bill. ]]> Belgium is pressing ahead with a new bill allowing police to potentially raid a person’s home suspected of harbouring an undocumented migrant.

Set for a vote next Thursday (4 November) in Belgium’s parliament, the law paves the wave for similar provisions in the EU’s deportation regulation.

Although Belgium abstained in the vote on the EU-level law given internal objections over possible EU deportation facilities abroad, Belgium’s coalition government appears determined to allow authorities to force their way into homes.

Read more

Police will get powers to raid homes in new EU deportation bill

The new law, championed by Belgium’s rightwing migration minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt of the N-VA, has triggered widespread criticism.

A spectrum form human rights defenders to Belgian judges have issued multiple warnings that the law would potentially violate constitutional rights of those who host undocumented immigrants.

If a person is suspected of hosting an undocumented migrant deemed a security threat, then the police can enter their home between 5AM and 9PM and search through their documents and personal belongings even if children are present.

    ]]>         Culture groups ‘on their knees’ after 30% funding cut proposed in EU’s next budget https://euobserver.com/245996/culture-groups-on-their-knees-after-30-funding-cut-proposed-in-next-eus-budget/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:05:12 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245996 Culture, media and rights groups demand that European capitals oppose a 30 percent cut to €8.6bn proposed for AgoraEU in the EU's next long-term budget. “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP.]]> “Thirty percent, we won’t consent” chants echoed across Schuman roundabout in the Brussels European quarter this week, as culture, media and journalist workers demanded that national leaders halt plans to reduce cash for culture in a protest on Thursday (29 October).

    Representatives from European rights forums, culture groups and a journalism federation gathered in a bid to keep enough money flowing to their organisations.

    “There’s a very grim future if we continue with these cuts,” said Rhys Nugent of Culture Action Europe, one of the protest’s organisers. “These sectors are already on their knees.”

    The demonstration came after EU leaders discussed giving less money than previously proposed to AgoraEU, an umbrella for culture, media, democracy and rights initiatives, within the EU’s 2028-2034 budget.

    30% less for culture

    Reacting to the EU Commission’s proposal to give AgoraEU €8.6bn under the long-term budget, the EU parliament’s budget committee asked to ramp this up to €10.7bn.

    But national capitals have not agreed to either proposal.

    Instead, the Irish presidency of Council presented a plan earlier this month (October 10) to allocate €5.3bn for AgoraEU –  representing a 30 percent cut to the commission’s proposal. It was responding to pressures for frugality from some member states.

    National capitals are yet to finalise a budget agreement.

    Read more

    Pressure mounts on EU leaders to strike a budget deal by December

    “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP and chair of parliament’s culture and education committee.

    “If this goes through, people will wake up one day and ask: why are my rights not protected? Why has that film festival disappeared? Where has my local publisher gone?” she said.

    “These cuts will save only a tiny percent of the EU budget but cause massive damage to these sectors,” added the German lawmaker. 

    What could be chopped?

    AgoraEU is a new umbrella for Creative Europe and Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV).

    Protest organiser Nugent said Creative Europe “funds everything from small theatrical productions to large cooperation around Europe.”

    He pointed to Flow, an Oscar-winning film, Europa Cinemas, and Culture Moves Europe as examples of the types of bodies that could be affected by a lack of EU funding.

    ]]>         Listen: Why is the EU introducing a new €2 charge on parcels? https://euobserver.com/245922/listen-why-is-the-eu-introducing-a-new-e2-charge-on-parcels/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:36:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245922 From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.

    So why is the EU doing this, and what difference will it make? Let’s start with what’s changing.

    From this Sunday, there will be a €2 tax on each product category contained in a parcel coming from outside the EU. This ads up to the €3 tax on small parcels introduced in June this year. So for a parcel of less than €150, you can already count a €5 charge, and that’s if your parcel contains just one category of item.

    Say you order four different garments from the Chinese platform Shein. The total charge comes to €20.

    Officially, it’s the sellers who are supposed to pay, not consumers. But in practice, they pass the cost on to customers one way or another.

    So why this second charge? The €3 charge adopted in June was meant to tackle the flood of small parcels coming from companies like Temu and Shein.

    Parcels of very low value, often just a few euros. And that’s not an exaggeration. According to Kristian Vanderwaeren, Belgium’s head of customs, the average value of a parcel before the charge was around €5.     CIB is a manipulative communication tactic that uses a combination of authentic, fake and duplicated social media accounts to operate as an adversarial network across platforms such as X, Facebook or Bluesky.

    By coordinating their activity, these accounts can amplify particular messages and create an online impression that may not reflect the reality of public opinion.

    The tactic spread massively during Covid.

    In a paper entitled ‘Coordinated inauthentic behavior: An innovative manipulation tactic to amplify Covid-19 anti-vaccine communication outreach via social media’, Monica Murero wrote that such operations could be “one of the greatest threats to freedom of expression and democracy in our society”.

    But this distortion becomes particularly visible during elections.

    Indeed, with political momentum, spreading messages and content online can influence how voters perceive the strength of an incumbent government and the prospects of its opposition.

    Manufacturing political dominance

    The latest example is Serbia.

    Ahead of parliamentary elections in Serbia, the Balkan Free Media Initiative (BFMI), in collaboration with Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub, investigated how coordinated networks promoted former Serbian PM and president Aleksandar Vučić while undermining independent media.

    “CIB corrupts the public signal that democracies rely on to understand themselves,” head of research at BFMI Vanesa Valcheva told EUobserver.

    The findings point to a broader problem for democratic debate: online visibility can be manipulated to sustain an image of political dominance, even when the picture on the ground appears different.

    “Incumbents often try to look unbeatable to discourage opposition voters, reassure their supporters, and show outside partners that things are unlikely to change,” Valcheva said.

    Before the rise of these coordinated online operations, the digital space offered dissent more room to breathe.

    But nowadays, CIB networks can undermine the online space by repeatedly circulating messages that support a particular political interest and make it appear more widely shared than it is.

    And indeed, Vučić dominated the space on X and Facebook while the streets suggested otherwise.

The question that will outlast the result is not who wins, but whether the winner is willing to say no to prime minister Rumen Radev.

    Radev spent nine years as president with Iliana Yotova as his vice-president.

    He resigned in January to enter party politics and the office passed to her automatically; she has never been elected to it.

    In April his Progressive Bulgaria coalition won 131 of parliament’s 240 seats, and it now backs her for a full term.

    In the first round she led Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, by fewer than three points. Turnout was 22 percent – the lowest on record.

    Read more

    [Interview] Bulgaria’s presidential election becomes a test of Rumen Radev’s grip on power

    The presidency’s power to say no

    An elected majority is legitimate; so is cooperation between government and president. The constitutional risk begins where cooperation becomes an expectation of loyalty. An institution can keep every legal power and still lose the will to use it against political allies.

    In Bulgaria those powers are modest but real.

    A president can send a law back, and parliament must debate and vote on it again in public. Radev’s majority can pass it a second time with 121 votes, but the second vote is on the record.

    A president can also refer a law to the Constitutional Court, commands the armed forces, and chairs the Consultative Council on National Security, where the state assesses threats to itself.

    None of this can stop a determined majority. All of it can force one to explain itself.

    Black Sea test came late

    Meanwhile, since the start of October, at least seven merchant ships have been hit by drones off the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts.

    Both governments suspect Russian involvement, although responsibility has not been conclusively established; more than two dozen sailors are dead or missing.

    Read more

    EU unlikely to send Black Sea naval mission to repel Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian grain ships, despite Kallas’ support

    The first strike in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone came on 6 October. By then Yotova had been president for nine months without once convening the security council. She convened it the next day, after the opposition demanded it in public.

    It condemned the attacks and endorsed better surveillance and counter-drone defences: the right decisions, taken after the pressure rather than before the risk.

    Her legislative record points the same way.

    Yotova knows how to use a veto: in February she returned an Electoral Code amendment that limited the number of polling stations in countries outside the EU, calling it unconstitutional.

    That parliament was not Radev’s. Against his majority the test came in July, with the 2026 budget. The reformist and conservative opposition, the Podkrepa trade union and a petition with more than 32,000 signatures asked her to return it. Y

    Yotova argued that a veto would deepen financial uncertainty and promulgated the budget. On 20 October, the Constitutional Court upheld the budget as a whole but struck down two provisions inserted through it. The challenge came from MPs and the ombudsman, not the presidency.

    Nato dispute

    One policy dispute between the candidates concerns Article 4 of the Nato treaty. Gyurov wants Bulgaria to request consultations with its allies. Yotova initially opposed invoking it, but later acknowledged that coordinated action with other allies remained an option.

    Radev ruled it out on the day of the first attack because the ships were struck outside Bulgarian territorial waters. Yet Article 4 does not require an attack on national territory; it applies whenever an ally considers its security threatened. Whether to invoke it is a political choice. Territorial eligibility is not the obstacle.

    The test of an independent presidency is not whether it agrees with the government on Article 4. It is whether it would demand a public account of what the state knew, what it did and what went wrong, and publish it even when it embarrasses the people who put it in office.

    The European Commission’s rule-of-law report in July noted that most of Bulgaria’s regulators had their mandates renewed without becoming any more independent. A renewed mandate is not proof of oversight. Neither is a convened council.

    The same test applies to Gyurov, an independent nominated by the reformist parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, who told CNN on 23 October that Bulgaria needs a counterweight to its government.     EU leaders condemned the attacks at their 15–16 October summit, and Nato has announced additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones.

    Both are entitled to a clear account of what Bulgaria saw, when it acted and what failed.

    Brussels, for its part, should judge institutional independence not by formal procedures, but by whether those institutions are willing to challenge those in power. The question to ask is simpler: when did it last contradict the government?

    Radev has a mandate to govern. The next president will hold a separate one: to question, to return, to refer and, when necessary, to refuse.

    Europe does not need a Bulgaria that pretends it never makes mistakes. It needs one that can find and correct them before its sailors, its neighbours and its allies pay for them.

    But the EIA argues that neither decision is backed up by evidence that the rules actually threaten Europe’s energy supply or push up prices.

    By delaying a law already adopted in 2024, the group says, the commission is “undermining integrity of both the legislative process and the EU rule of law.”

    “Rather than ensuring that the EU Methane Regulation is implemented as agreed, the commission has responded to pressure from the fossil-fuel industry by weakening enforcement and proposing further delays, without providing credible evidence to justify these decisions,” said Jack Corscadden, senior climate campaigner at EIA.

      <title>The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/31/elon-musk-midterms-spending-visualized</link>
      <description><p>The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history</p><p>Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jan/03/tesla-diner-elon-musk-los-angeles">Tesla Diner in Los Angeles</a>, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.</p><p>Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/31/elon-musk-midterms-spending-visualized">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough</p><p>A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 01 Nov 2026 15:46:38 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Can you really ‘make your money back’ on UK pension in two years and eight months?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/01/can-you-really-make-your-money-back-on-uk-pension-in-two-years-and-eight-months/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/01/can-you-really-make-your-money-back-on-uk-pension-in-two-years-and-eight-months/Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:22:44 +0000I’m still confused about a UK pensions article you wrote some time back. The person had 20 years of contributions and it takes 35 years to get a full pension, so a difference of 15 years.

Are you saying that if she now pays Class 3 contributions of £956.80 for the next 15 years (costing her not too far off £15k), she will have that £15k back after drawing the pension for two years and eight months?

R O’N

It all seems a bit fantastic but, in pure maths terms, that is exactly how it works. However, there are a couple of “real world” issues you need to take into account that will skew that simplicity.

We will come to that in a bit, but first let’s crunch the numbers.

Hundreds of thousands of Irish people – possibly millions – have spent time working in the UK at some point in their careers before returning home or moving on elsewhere. The fact that they could be entitled to a weekly UK state pension – currently paid at £241.30 (€288.50) a week – could make a big difference to some of them.

In 2026/27 – the current UK tax year – it will cost you £18.40 a week to buy back Class 3 national insurance contributions to boost your UK pension. That comes to £956.80 (€1,145.50) a year.

Regular readers will be aware that the cheaper Class 2 contributions many paid to buy back up to 18 years over cover recently are no longer available to people paying voluntary national insurance from abroad. So Class 3 is where we are at from now on.

The current full UK state pension is, as I said, £241.30 and each year you buy back will add £6.89 per week – one thirty-fifth of 241.30 – to the pension you eventually receive at today’s prices. That amounts to £358.28 extra in pension over the course of a year.

Pensions: The most important step is simply getting started

To find out how long it will take you to “make back” what you have paid in, you simple divide the £956.80 cost by the extra pension you get on the back of it – £358.28. That gives you a figure of 2.67 per cent, or just a shade over two years and eight months.

For someone buying back 15 years, the same holds true: you are simply multiplying both the contributions and the benefit by a factor of 15 so you are not changing the math.

But now we come to where reality intrudes into the basic math.

The contributions you are paying come from already taxed income. As in Ireland national insurance is a form of tax, with a small “t”. But the money you receive in retirement will likely be liable for income tax and USC in Ireland, assuming you live here.

If you are paying income tax at 20 per cent, the extra pension amount into your hand each year for every additional year’s contribution you make drops to £286.62. On that basis it would take you 3.35 years, three years and about four months, to make back what you paid in.

If you pay tax at 40 per cent, the benefit in your pocket falls to £214.97 a year for each year’s additional contribution. On that basis, you would not be in “profit” on the arrangement until 4.45 years after you draw down the pension – close to 4½ years.

How to navigate and maximise Ireland’s State pension

USC will extend that again but, given the multiple rates, I’m not going into that in detail. Suffice to say that it will extend the “pay back” period slightly.

However, on average, an Irish man can expect to live for 15 years in retirement and a woman almost 19, so it still seems like a good idea.

There are a couple of other issues that clearly affect the precise payback time.

One is that you are dealing with currency risk. There is no way of putting a figure on this but, clearly, the euro/sterling exchange rates when you make the payment and when you eventually draw down the pension will be different. Whether that benefits you or penalises you, only time can tell.

Then you need to remember that both the pension payable and the cost of these Class 3 contributions tend to change each year. For instance, the full UK pension rate will rise to £250.70 a week.

You do also need to bear in mind that the British are once again fiddling with how they work out pension increases – largely because the current “triple lock” is proving expensive in the context of other demands on exchequer funds.

Your pension: how to make up for lost time

As of now, the tiple locks guarantees that the state pension will rise by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5 per cent. From April 2030, unless things change again between now and then, the link to earnings is gone – leaving pension increases to rise by 2.5 per cent or the rate of inflation, whichever is higher.

The expectation, certainly in Whitehall, is that this will reduce the scale of annual pension increases.

That all makes it difficult to be absolutely definitive on these things but, given that the UK state pension this woman receives in 15 years time (or whenever she subsequently retires) will be higher than it is today, it will in fact take less than the time given above to recover her outlay.

Of course, that does have to be offset against the “opportunity cost” – what return that money might have delivered if invested other than in buying back UK pension years – but we’re definitely not getting into that here.

There is one other issue that might skew the numbers. The 35-year timeline for people to secure a full UK state pension is based on someone who starts paying national insurance in 2016 when the new system came into force.

Of course, for the majority of Irish – and others – who are considering voluntary contributions, their UK national insurance record will have started earlier, many decades earlier in some cases. Under the old system, as I understand it, people could secure a full basic state pension on the back of 30 years contribution – but those who retired on this pension before 2016 receive a lower weekly payment.

So they really need to get a fix on what their UK pension position is.

According to the UK government website, they will work out your starting (2016) position under the new state pension. You will be entitled to the higher of the amount you would have got under the old system or the amount you would qualify for under the new system if it had been in place when you started making contributions.

This is important because you then know how many years of contributions you need to make on a voluntary basis to qualify for the maximum pension. It might not be as straightforward as “I worked there for 20 years, so I need another 15 years of voluntary contributions”... or it might.

Confusing? Yep, but that’s what happens when a country changes the way it calculates pension rights.

Anyway, to get a definitive answer, you can check your current pension situation with the UK authorities. There is a user-friendly online system but it does require a UK government ID which many who once worked in the UK will not have.

The alternatives are to contract them via a dedicated email form they provide, though they do warn that it is taking some time to reply to emails.

You can also try phoning – at +44 (0)191 2187777 – though regular readers will be aware of my view that confirmation in writing is always a good idea. Or you can write to them at: The Pension Service 11, Mail Handling Site A, Wolverhampton, WV98 1LW, England.

Please send your queries to Dominic Coyle, Q&A, The Irish Times, 24-28 Tara Street, Dublin 2, or by email to dominic.coyle@irishtimes.com with a contact phone number. This column is a reader service and is not intended to replace professional advice.

New Government investment accounts could generate up to €400m in fees for banks

“Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.

The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its Futures Insurance Fund and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said ​on X.

]]>Dan Kitwood<![CDATA[‘Seville is still a lot cheaper than Ireland. When Kerry-born Gráinne Walsh went to Seville to study at the Universidad de Sevilla on an Erasmus programme in 1996, she found love in the form of a local man, Alfonso. Thirty years on the couple have raised a family of four children and are enjoying all the attractions of living in the historic southern Spanish city.

Walsh’s first spell in Seville was part of a wider international business and languages degree at DCU. She fell in love with the city straight away.

“I came in mid-September and loved the blue skies and warm weather. A bottle of decent wine cost 350 pesetas (about €2). You could go out at 11pm when you would be coming home from the pub at home.”

Walsh returned to Dublin to finish her degree, but Alfonso soon followed to ask for her hand in marriage.

“I was only 20 at the time; he was 27. I let my heart rule my head. I said yes, but on one condition. I needed to travel before I settled down. I went off travelling the world on a student travel deal from Usit. I rang him from Ayers Rock on a mobile phone the size of a brick, saying, “Don’t panic. I have not found a local man and I’ll be back soon.”

A Wicklow woman in Marbella: ‘I would make friends in the summer and they would then go home. But I found my tribe’

Walsh was keen to secure a professional role in Seville so she researched companies with Irish links. She found a marketing position at a local brewer, Cruzcampo, then a subsidiary of Guinness, and later purchased by Heineken.

“My name Gráinne was unpronounceable. They ended up calling me Walsh. I went on to positions in HR and corporate relations. I had the best job in the house and enjoyed every day.

“Cruzcampo is an institution locally, a company where people stay for life and I spent almost 20 years there. Working there was a great experience for me but, by 2017, I had a hankering to do something else.”

Walsh undertook a master’s in coaching and, by 2019, felt confident to strike out on her own. Covid soon struck, but she was able to secure coaching business online and also found a part-time academic position as an associate professor at Universidad Loyola, where she lectures on business degree programmes.

Today, her work also involves leadership training programmes for corporates. A core part of her work involves teaching participants soft skills such as assertiveness, empathy and emotional intelligence. Among her multinational clients is Navantia, the owners of Harland & Wolff shipbuilders, and her work takes her to Britain and Ireland as well as the rest of Spain.

Walsh says the workplace culture in Spain has traditionally been very macho and less progressive than in Ireland but this is beginning to change.

“Spanish women have faced significant challenges. In the corporate world, they have been trying to juggle balls, being the perfect professional while also being a good wife and mother. Fortunately, thanks to Covid, there’s more acceptance of remote working and work-life balance and things are starting to improve.”

From Navan to Valencia: ‘They refer to the Irish here as the Latins of the north’

Life in Seville is good, and Walsh says it has been a safe city to raise their children who are aged 16-22. She loves its traditions, especially around holy week at Easter and says April is a beautiful time to visit when Seville’s famous orange trees blossom.

“For me it’s a perfect-sized city. Its big but not too big. You can walk around it safely. It’s small enough to be spontaneous. You can say to someone that you will meet them in 15 minutes.

“The tourist boom, though, means that locals now have to do the unthinkable and make reservations in their favourite restaurants.”

The significant increase in tourism in recent years has also been accompanied with concern about rising property prices, with locals often priced out of the market. Mirroring other parts of Spain, this has added fuel to the social unrest as a result of big cost of living increases in recent years.

“Inflation has definitely hit in, but it is still a lot cheaper than Ireland. You can still buy a coffee for €1.80.”

The family live in a town house on the edge of the city centre, featuring the essential ingredients of air conditioning and a pool in the back garden to escape Seville’s hot summers. Weekends are often spent down at the coast in Huelva.

People in Seville are either Huelva beachgoers or Cadiz beach goers, she says. While they are both on the Atlantic, Huelva has a more relaxed family vibe, while Cadiz attracts young surfers and those seeking a livelier night scene.

“Social life is outdoors 10 months of the year. We like to sail and we have a boat in Huelva, which is our floating house.”

Walsh misses the easy hospitable and warm personality of the Irish but has no intention of returning home.

“I do miss the green fields of Ireland. We did an extended house exchange with my parents when the kids were very young and spent some time in Cahersiveen.

“I worried about what would happen if I fell in love with the Irish lifestyle. Two weeks into the grey skies and pouring rain of south Kerry, that decision about where we would live became a lot easier.”

]]>BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI<![CDATA[It’s inflation, stupid: Trump faces the wrath of US voters ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/31/its-inflation-stupid-trump-faces-the-wrath-of-us-voters/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/31/its-inflation-stupid-trump-faces-the-wrath-of-us-voters/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000On Tuesday the United States will hold a referendum on Donald Trump. The Republican Party has become the Trump Party, which means the careers of dozens of Republican politicians are tethered to him. The party of Abraham Lincoln depends on a man cut from very different clobber. If the polls are to be believed, “The Donald” is over, with ratings the lowest ever for a sitting president heading into the midterms.
