No one said this was going to end well. Indeed, the party’s civil war is unlikely to end when Trump leaves office. His influence is likely to mutate into something possibly even more divisive as he tries to make sure that his chosen Make America Great Again (Maga) successor maintains his legacy and keeps his sons out of jail.

Meanwhile, the US will be left with the largest debt burden in its history, which is being added to every year with a huge budget deficit funded by issuing yet more debt. While not quite a Ponzi scheme, the US is moving in the Ponzi direction. By paying the interest on the debt by raising yet more debt, even Washington is vulnerable. What happens to the dollar if the foreigners who are buying this US debt, and in the process help keep the dollar pre-eminent, decide to cut their positions before those positions become losses?

Medium-term worries about US debt splurges are becoming more acute by the week. But for Tuesday’s plebiscite, the immediate issue is prices, particularly petrol prices. To paraphrase James Carville’s “it’s the economy, stupid” maxim from 1992, in 2026, “it’s inflation, stupid”. Inflation has been rising in the US, squeezing the car-driving suburban middle classes. At the same time, the one thing that really makes Americans feel wealthy – the price of their homes – has been going in the wrong direction.

The median house price dipped to $419,250 in September 2026 (down 1.2 per cent year-over-year), marking 11 consecutive months of declines as sellers slash asking prices. About one fifth of all houses listed on the market have seen their asking prices fall in the last year. This affects the perception of wealth among the 61 per cent of Americans who own their own homes. The fact that the Democrats – a party in disarray – hold a 9-point edge over the Republican Party among likely voters, with 53 per cent of them saying they are voting or leaning towards the Dems, tells you how far Trump has fallen.

What’s going on?

The US is experiencing what economists call a K-shaped economy: the gains of the growth are going to the richest people, while those at the bottom fall behind. The reasons are that the tax system has been changed to reward those at the top and the stock market, owned far more by the richest Americans, has been soaring.

For example, over the past four years since the end of the pandemic, house prices have flatlined but the Standard & Poor’s 500 index is up 131 per cent. The profits from the US tech boom have largely ended up in the pockets of the already wealthy, while real wages have fallen and tariffs imposed by Trump have increased the price of imported consumer goods, squeezing the middle earner that bit more.

What happens in Israeli and US elections may reshape the Middle East

A lot, but not all of this, is Trump’s fault.

His war in Iran was a turning point. Americans are not usually too bothered by foreign policy, but the immediate increase in petrol prices when the Strait of Hormuz closed has tied Trump to faltering disposable income. With higher energy prices pushing up inflation, the average dude on the street copped it. Even his once loyal supporters have gone off him since February. Only 67 per cent of 2024 Trump supporters now approve of him, down from 75 per cent in July, 83 per cent at the beginning of this year and 95 per cent early in his second term.

With energy prices rising, the Federal Reserve could not cut interest rates, even if Trump wanted it to. Almost the first thing Kevin Warsh, Trump’s Federal Reserve chair appointee, did was raise interest rates, pushing mortgage rates to 7.3 per cent from 6 per cent this time last year. All these little increases in prices or interest rates hurt and dent the feel-good factor.

Electricity prices are also rising, and Trump – an AI evangelist – is being associated with data centres that are gobbling up the grid’s capacity, so the price the average person pays for electricity is perceived to be strongly affected by AI companies. This is not a good look for a populist president, not least because the tech-bro aristocracy who run Silicon Valley are among the most despised groups in US popular culture.

Speaking of culture wars, some heat has been taken out of issues like immigration. The president’s policy has been successful in the sense that illegal immigration has plummeted. Immigration was the top problem for 28 per cent of Americans in Gallup’s Feb 2024 poll, when worries about the economy and inflation were 12 per cent and 11 per cent respectively. By September 2026, only 10 per cent of Americans picked immigration as an issue. Economic worries keep more than a third of voters awake.

Fed holds US interest rates ahead of midterm elections

If the polls are right, is this the end of the Trump era, in the sense that he ceases to be the central character in US politics? If he loses both the Senate and the House, the presidential race starts. A battle for the heart and soul of the Republican Party will ensue between the baseball cap and the golf club, between Maga and penny-loafer America.

It is a great opportunity for the Democrats, but that party is riven by a generational war – the Clintonistas versus the Zoranistas, the old versus the young, the radical sons versus the centrist dads.

Take your seats, the main event hasn’t even started yet.

]]><![CDATA[Jack Chambers ‘disappointed’ as WRC says public sector pay talks at ‘an impasse’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/31/talks-between-unions-and-government-over-new-pay-deal-finish-without-agreement/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/31/talks-between-unions-and-government-over-new-pay-deal-finish-without-agreement/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:52:29 +0000Talks between the public sector unions and the Government on certain aspects of a new pay deal have reached “an impasse”, the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) said on Saturday.

The prospect of a second national public service strike grew on Friday evening as talks between Government representatives and union leaders at concluded without agreement.

In a statement on Saturday morning, the WRC said it was requesting that the Government-appointed group led by Kevin Foley consider certain issues and “put forward a means of resolution”.

“Having engaged in intensive talks for 10 days, under the auspices of the WRC the commission is of the view that certain matters have reached an impasse and is requesting that the Government-appointed group consider those issues and put forward a means of resolution,” it said.

“All other matters under discussion shall remain with the WRC. As talks have yet to conclude, all discussions will continue to remain confidential to the parties.”

Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said he was disappointed by the progress.

“I am disappointed that, despite intensive negotiations over the last 10 days public service pay discussions have not yet delivered an agreed outcome,” he said.

“I recognise the efforts of all parties over recent weeks and thank the WRC for its role in supporting these discussions.

“Government remains committed to agreeing a fair and credible pay deal for workers across the public service that is also affordable and sustainable for the country.”

Speaking as the talks ended at about 11.30pm, Kevin Callinan, general secretary of Fórsa, said it had become clear that the gap between the two sides was too great to close at this stage and, with no further talks planned for over the weekend, he and the other trade union participants in the process would now brief the other public service unions on Monday.

“It doesn’t seem possible at this moment that we’re going to be able to reach an agreement that we could confidently put to our members in a ballot so our next step is to meet with our affiliate unions on Monday morning, where we’ll brief them on the negotiations, and decide on what comes next,” he said.

How can the public sector pay deal get over the line?

Asked if it was possible the two sides would be brought back together under the auspices of the Kevin Foley-led committee appointed to help resolve the outstanding difficulties that had originally prevented the talks getting started, Callinan said that was a matter for the WRC but that the unions would remain available and would attend any process initiated.

“But we really need to be confident that any proposals would be likely to be accepted by members of the ballot, and we’re a long way from that,” he said.

He said the union side had been consistent from the outset with regard to the issues that needed to be addressed by Government in terms of the gap between pay increases and inflation over the past five years, an increase for the second half of this year and measures to ensure members were protected against spikes in inflation over the course of any new deal and agreement.

A second national public services strike will be scheduled for Wednesday, November 11th, if no deal between the Government and trade unions on a new pay agreement is reached over the weekend, Callinan said earlier.

Callinan, who is also chair of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions’ public services committee, said the 19 unions it encompasses should meet on Monday to get an update on the talks and, if no agreement has been reached by then, to discuss taking further action.

He said the strike, which would again close the State’s schools and severely affect health, local authority and other services, would allow for demonstrations in Dublin and other big urban centres by more than 300,000 staff affected.

In an earlier update to the 100,000 members of his own union, Callinan said the talks had been “lengthy and at times heated” and that while a deal remains possible “the Government has yet to put forward a credible offer, and it remains to be seen whether it will do so”.

The Claude Code revenue take-off was a sign that Anthropic had found “product/market fit”, the moment when a technology meets a particular need and demand takes off. But beyond coding, Anthropic and its rivals are still searching for ways to unlock a much bigger market.

The recent slowdown is also a reminder that, unlike traditional software companies, little of Anthropic’s revenue is tied to regular subscriptions. In the first half of this year, 83 per cent came from consumption, making it highly dependent on short-term usage.

Sanofi gained 4.71 per cent after the French pharmaceutical firm reported third-quarter results ahead of analyst expectations ​and lifted its outlook.

Among other movers, Bayer gained 5.46 per cent after winning a ​trial on Thursday over claims by three women that its Roundup weedkiller caused their cancer.

New York

By the close of trading in Europe, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index had fallen 3.5 per cent, on track for its worst month since March 2025, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.8 per cent.

Amazon shares slumped 2.1 per cent, as the company’s AI spending plans and lagging ecommerce business overshadowed solid growth in cloud sales in the eyes of investors after it reported earnings on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Intel was eyeing its worst one-day drop on record after the chipmaker reported a revenue forecast that missed analysts’ estimates, hurt by sputtering demand for PC processors and supply-chain problems with its lucrative data-centre components. Shares fell 30 per cent.

Intel’s rivals Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia were down 12 per cent and 4.6 per cent respectively.

Outside of tech, ExxonMobil Holdings reported earnings before the bell on Friday that surpassed expectations on the strength of surging gasoline and diesel prices that pushed refining results to an all-time high. The shares gained 1.8 per cent. Chevron also beat expectations, sending shares up 1.6 per cent. – Additional reporting by Reuters

Last May, the High Court dismissed a challenge to the grant of planning permission given by An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to EDF Renewables Ireland Ltd for the turbines in an area of Carlow known as Killeshin Hills, Ridge, Agharue, Coonnakishna and Seskinrea.

The challenge had been brought by information technology professional Stephen Keogh, who lives a few kilometres from the proposed development, and by farmer Tom Quirke, who lives less than a kilometre from the site. A non-governmental organisation called the Rural Residents Wind Aware and Environmental Group also brought the challenge.

Following its decision, the challengers then asked the High Court for leave to appeal its decision to the Court of Appeal, but this was refused.

The challengers then sought a direct appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds that the case raised matters of public importance or was in the interests of justice. ACP opposed granting leave to appeal while EDF was a notice party.

A central point of the challengers’ argument was the application of the Government’s 2006 rules for wind farm developments, the Wind Energy Development Guidelines. These are not binding but are matters to which ACP is required to have regard in making its decisions.

The Supreme Court said the objectors had essentially maintained that the separation distances between the seven turbines did not comply with requirements of the guidelines. This provides that any proposed layout of wind turbines takes into account the development potential of an adjoining site for a similar development.

The Supreme Court said the High Court, in its decision, had not misapplied the guidelines.

In a written determination, the Supreme Court refused to grant an appeal.

The court did not consider that the application for an appeal met the constitutional criteria of public importance and interests of justice.

It said it should be observed that the ACP inspector and ACP itself were only “to have regard” to the guidelines, “which they clearly did”.

]]>Narumon Bowonkitwanchai<![CDATA[‘No evidence’ Bawag’s €1.6bn PTSB offer is ‘bad deal for shareholders’, court told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/no-evidence-bawags-16bn-ptsb-offer-is-bad-deal-for-shareholders-court-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/no-evidence-bawags-16bn-ptsb-offer-is-bad-deal-for-shareholders-court-told/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:01:10 +0000There is “simply no evidence” that the €1.6 billion proposal from Austrian lender Bawag to acquire PTSB for €2.97 a share “is a bad deal for shareholders”, the High Court has heard, while it remains the “only price on offer” despite “musings and mutterings” otherwise.

There is “not a jot of evidence to suggest the Minister [for Finance] was motivated by anything other than price” when he voted in favour of the bid, which would see the end of the State’s ownership of Ireland’s third largest bank, Lyndon MacCann, counsel for the Minister, told Judge Michael Quinn on Friday.

Then minister for finance Brian Lenihan jnr, when buying 99.2 per cent of PTSB in 2011, did so “not for some opportunistic commercial venture”, but “to come to the aid of a flailing bank during a time of financial crisis”, MacCann told the court.

The proposed takeover of PTSB by Bawag, which is subject to High Court approval, has been before the court this week. Proceedings were dominated by objections to the deal from four minority shareholders who, collectively, own 0.00287 per cent of the bank.

They allege the acquisition should not be sanctioned as, among other reasons, the Minister benefits from “special, incredible” rights not enjoyed by other shareholders, which led to unequal access to information during the bid’s consultation process.

However, to argue this point “involved turning logic on its head”, MacCann said.

Piotr Skocylas, a litigating shareholder who has addressed the court for the past four days, briefly questioned the constitutionality of the Minister’s holding of PTSB shares on Thursday. He has repeatedly lamented the way in which he acquired his current 57.5 per cent stake.

Shareholders have acquired their stake in the company through various different means, he said, with some buying, inheriting or being given their shares at various different prices.

“Irrespective of how we got here, we got here lawfully,” MacCann said.

He added that Skocylas “has not put any evidence before that court that the scheme is a bad deal for shareholders”.

“All he has put before the court is photocopies of two reports,” he said, citing an S&P newsletter and Business Post article, which quote financial analysts’ opinions on the acquisition offer.

“They are entitled to their view, but this is not evidence that an intelligent or honest member of the class could not have reasonably voted in favour of the scheme,” MacCann said, citing the legal threshold for the scheme to be approved.

The litigating shareholders also claim the Minister was swayed in favour of the bid for commercial and somewhat political reasons, such as Bawag’s assertion that PTSB’s headquarters would remain in Dublin and there would be little to no change in its branch footprint. This, they say, has resulted in the Minister opting for a “derisory” price point.

But MacCann said share price was the “dominant motivator” behind the Minister’s support. “The only price on offer is the price offered by Bawag,” he said. “That is the best price because there is no other price on offer.”

Meanwhile, Axis Capital “is not within a country mile” of preparing a tangible counter offer, MacCann said in court, despite “mutterings and musings” from the advisory firm cofounded by Mark Duffy, the former chief executive of Bank of Scotland Ireland.

Last Thursday the firm said it would seek an adjournment of this week’s High Court proceedings of up to six weeks to allow time for it to prepare a rival bid. The court heard on Wednesday Axis could offer €3.20 per share by way of a bid supported by “one of the most esteemed investment banks in the world”.

Kelley Smith, counsel for PTSB, told the court Axis “lacks the resources to actually implement an offer” and “has no track record of M&A [merger and acquisition] transactions”.

“Axis is a €100 company,” she said, pointing to financial accounts for the year ended May 2026 that “showed €100 on its balance sheet”.

]]><![CDATA[New Government investment accounts could generate up to €400m in fees for banks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/new-investment-accounts-could-generate-up-to-400m-in-fees-for-banks/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/new-investment-accounts-could-generate-up-to-400m-in-fees-for-banks/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:14:08 +0000Personal investment accounts (PIAs) could generate up to €400 million in additional fee income for banks and other providers by 2035, according to Davy Stockbrokers.

The brokerage estimated that, at peak, up to €4 billion in annual investment could flow into these accounts “although the path to this level is uncertain”.

This presented “a potentially meaningful fee opportunity for providers able to capture the flow”, it said.

Greater administrative, tax and reporting requirements in Ireland would favour “scaled providers” such as banks and life assurance companies, Davy said. Online brokers are also expected to offer accounts.

“Applying a range of fee outcomes to our annual flow assumptions implies €100-€400 million of annual fee income by 2035, with the opportunity building as PIA assets accumulate,” it said.

“The onboarding and administrative requirements for PIAs should favour established providers over smaller, more niche providers, resulting in the Irish banks as natural beneficiaries,” Davy said.

Authors Thomas Ryan and Diarmaid Sheridan of Davy said the estimate of cumulative fees was based on an assumption that providers would charge 0.25-1 per cent of the account balance in annual fees.

They said the research was based on a number of assumptions about the number of people who might invest and their likely level of investment, which were based on existing savings and earnings data.

The new State-sponsored investment accounts, launched by Minister for Finance Simon Harris in the budget, will allow individuals to invest up to €12,000 a year in an account.

The accounts, which will be launched in July next year, will have a tax-free threshold of €50,000 after which a flat rate of 1 per cent will be charged.

Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?

The aim is to incentivise Irish savers to move some of the €170 billion held in low-interest-bearing deposit accounts back into capital markets.

Harris has described this money as “sitting idle”.

Davy said the scheme would “allow for a meaningful tax advantage relative to existing investment structures.”

“Our scenario analysis implies an effective tax rate of about 6 per cent over eight years compared with about 30 per cent for comparable investment vehicles,” it said.

The brokerage said the new scheme offered “a compelling economic proposition for investors” while noting international precedent pointed to a gradual adoption, with comparable UK and Swedish schemes having limited impact on existing savings patterns.

“PIAs should provide a welcome tailwind to Irish retail investing,” it said.

“We expect adoption to be gradual with flows captured at the margin from existing alternatives,” it said.

Recently published research from life insurance and pensions company Royal London Ireland looked at how much people believe they would set aside in the proposed PIA.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?

It suggested as many as six in 10 adults in Ireland could invest up to €250 per month in the scheme.

It also indicated that men, on average, expect to invest more than three times as much as women, at €893 per month compared with €240.

Harris first mooted his intention to introduce a new form of consumer-friendly investment account back in February.

His department is understood to have examined similar types of accounts operating in other countries. Ultimately, it opted largely for the Swedish model despite strong industry lobbying in favour of the rival UK individual savings account model.

   <title>Erste Risse in Vucics System</title>
   <description>Mehr als ein Jahrzehnt hat die rechtsnationalistische Serbische Fortschrittspartei (SNS) unter Aleksandar Vucic umfassende Kontrolle über Serbien ausgeübt. Nach dem herausragenden Sieg der Studentenliste (SL) am vergangenen Sonntag erhöhen nun die Studierenden den Druck auf Medien, Justiz und Politik, sich dem Machtwechsel zu beugen. In einigen Bereichen zeigen sich bereits Risse im alten System. Zugleich müsse die Studierendenbewegung tragfähige Strukturen aufbauen, sagte Serbien-Experte Jakov Devcic im ORF.at-Interview.</description>

President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis.

However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters.

pic.twitter.com/Gk4bPH1pJU

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 31, 2026

On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw.

At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors.

The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her.

pic.twitter.com/sni7uvIVke

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 30, 2026

Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”.

Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”.

Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”.

⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal.

Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence.

At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker.

The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon.

There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice.

Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026

Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners.

Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki.

Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”.

On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki.

@PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute.

Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w…

— Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026

Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted.

On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”.

Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki.

“One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.”

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki.

One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool.

Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw.

Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego.

Policja nie chce go przepuścić!

Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3

— Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026

The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening.

On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered.

The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence.

However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK.

“I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.”

Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,…

— Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026

Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański.

He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”.

That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties.

She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio.

Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995.

🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia”

– sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026

While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”.

“All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added.

Nastąpiło bezprawne przejęcie strony internetowej Trybunału Konstytucyjnego.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”.

 

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Tuesday, the Polish police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CBŚP) announced that anti-terrorism officers had detained the man, who can be named only as Artem S. under Polish privacy law, in Warsaw under a European Arrest Warrant issued by Romania.

In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company.

On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack.

The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.”

 

In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”.

Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania.

Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated.

Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.

Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026

In some cases, such operatives are amateurs – so-called “disposable agents” – recruited, coordinated and paid through messaging service Telegram. Some have also been pre-existing criminal groups hired by Russia to carry out such tasks.

In August, a drone production plant belonging to private Polish arms company WB Electronics was targeted in an arson attack that Poland has blamed on Russia.

The following month, a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was likewise hit by an arson attack that Poland blamed on Russia. Two Turkish men were later detained in Germany on suspicion of carrying out the attack.

Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”.

The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea.

The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership.

Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L

— Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) October 27, 2026

“Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw.

“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added.

His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine.

 

Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies.

Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones.

The Warsaw Defence Plan also pledges to “increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea”.

The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems.

Poland and the UK have signed a major new defence and security treaty.

The agreement includes plans to jointly develop a new air-defence missile, hold large-scale military exercises, and cooperate on countering Russian hybrid attacks https://t.co/cXeYT2u1lw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026

This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security.

Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year.

In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway.

In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal.

The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday.

Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”.

His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate.

Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid.

Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries.

Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.

She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.

Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.

Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.

Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.

Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany, while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.

Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026

Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań.

Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average.

Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20.

 

Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.”

Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia.

“I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports.

“We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”.

Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry.

The meeting was attended by representatives of 21 EU member states and European Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné. Discussions focused on protecting and strengthening European industry’s competitiveness and economic security amid geopolitical challenges.

“Today, we are facing the consequences of the fact that, in the past, competitiveness was often relegated to second, third or fourth place. Competitiveness took a back seat to other priorities, with the result that European industry now faces serious challenges,” said Domański.

He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition.

A former colleague of Polish President Karol Nawrocki from when he worked as a security guard in a hotel two decades ago testified in court that he told her it was possible to “make some extra money by bringing in girls”. She says she saw him escort a woman onto the premises.

The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot.

The court case began in September but, until now, hearings have been held behind closed doors. However, the judge decided that today’s session would be open to the public, with two former colleagues of Nawrocki giving evidence. The president himself is due to appear before the court in January.

🗣️ "Moją automatyczną oceną było, że to prostytutka i alfons."

Nowe zeznania w procesie Karola Nawrockiego z wydawcą Onetu. Przed sądem stanęła była współpracowniczka prezydenta z sopockiego Grand Hotelu. pic.twitter.com/Cn6KyMSjcv

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 27, 2026

In May last year, less than a week before the second round of the election, in which Nawrocki was standing in a run-off against rival Rafał Trzaskowski, Onet, a leading news website, published an article titled “Karol Nawrocki and the secrets of the Grand Hotel”.

It claimed, based on information provided by unnamed former colleagues of the future president, that he had “participated in bringing prostitutes for guests of the Grand Hotel in Sopot while working there as a security guard” almost 20 years earlier.

Onet said that its interlocutors wished to remain anonymous for their own safety, but had expressed their willingness to testify in court if required.

The revelations caused a major scandal, but were vigorously denied by Nawrocki, a conservative candidate aligned with the right-wing opposition, who called them a “pack of lies”. He then went on to narrowly defeat Trzaskowski in the election.

Conservative presidential candidate @NawrockiKn says he will sue news website @onetpl for claims it published today that he procured prostitutes for clients at a luxury hotel when working there as a security guard.

He called the report "a bunch of lies" https://t.co/WZ4rZWfFT1

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 26, 2025

Nawrocki then sued Ringier Axel Springer Polska (RASP), the Polish subsidiary of a German-Swiss media house that owns Onet, demanding an apology. RASP stood by Onet, saying that its reporting was “factual”.

At today’s hearing, one of Onet’s sources, Natasza Geldon, who worked at the hotel in 2006 and 2007, was questioned. She said that, one evening, she had noticed Nawrocki leading a man and a woman into the hotel, before then taking only the woman into a lift and returning alone.

This had struck her as unusual, because staff were not supposed to escort guests into the hotel, “let alone take them upstairs”, said Geldon, quoted by broadcaster TVP.

“When Karol came back downstairs, I asked him what was going on,” continued the witness. “He said it was possible to make some extra money by bringing girls in, and asked if I wanted to join in.”

Geldon refused the offer, telling the court that, “as a young girl, 19 years old, I had the impression that a pimp had been coming in with a prostitute”. However, when asked to confirm if she had seen prostitutes in the hotel, Geldon said: “I don’t know. It’s hard to say. It was just that one incident.”

 

A second witness, Łukasz Franczak, described as a longtime friend of Nawrocki who worked alongside him in security at the Grand Hotel, also gave evidence on Tuesday after being called by Nawrocki’s legal team.

He testified that there had been prostitutes in the hotel. However, he added that he had not heard of any organised operation to supply them to guests; nor had he witnessed Nawrocki procuring prostitutes or discussing payment for them, reported Onet from the hearing.

Franczak’s testimony was welcomed by Nawrocki’s former national security advisor, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, who said that it showed that those making claims against the president have no evidence of his involvement in any wrongdoing.

Oni się wszyscy teraz nakręcają jak szaleni, nie czytając tego co sami piszą na własnej stronie… No i dowiedzieli się dzisiaj, że w hotelach bywają prostytutki 🙂

A ja to wszystko czytam na bieżąco, a tam słynny Łukasz z Gdańska, ulubiony świadek-historyk Antka Dudka, i… https://t.co/9sKGZT4PpD

— Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) October 27, 2026

RASP’s lawyers have called for Nawrocki himself to testify in the case. The president’s legal team wanted him to provide his testimony in writing, according to Onet.

But on Tuesday, judge Aleksandra Orzechowska ordered Nawrocki to give testimony directly – either in person or remotely – at the next hearing, which is scheduled for 18 January 2027, reports broadcaster TVN.

Coupled with the Chancellor’s announcement of new investment in HMRC compliance activity which will see a further 670 compliance officers recruited by 2029-30, on top of the 5,500 previously announced, it paints a very clear picture. 

More compliance staff will mean HMRC is able to widen the net and spend more time poring over taxpayers affairs, looking at more players and possibly reaching down to more divisions below the Premier League.

There has already been a notable increase in HMRC compliance activity in sports in general, including not just football but also motorsport, boxing and other individual sports such as tennis and golf. But the announcements this week signal that this scrutiny is likely to increase over the next few years. 

Major risk area for HMRC

Football specifically is seen as a major risk area for HMRC, and the new report on modernising the approach to “wealthy taxpayers”, defined as those with income over £200,000 or assets of over £2m, means that more of the UK’s top sports professionals could face more investigations from the revenue.  

The small print also shows that HMRC will collate information from open sources. It is already common practice to use news articles and press interviews against taxpayers when their words conflict with tax statements.  

However, high-profile people, such as footballers, face their social media channels increasingly being checked by HMRC, where careless posts or even words could well lead to misunderstandings or challenges.

Additionally, there will be more pooling of resources and collating additional information on this group of taxpayers to ensure greater tax compliance. In football, this is likely to mean bringing together those with knowledge of clubs’ and agents’ affairs, for example, with those focused on individual players.

Taxed on your reel?

Given greater global tax transparency we also expect HMRC to bring in information received from other jurisdictions on players’ affairs which will result in much more involved, and potentially expensive, compliance checks for them and indeed other sportspeople.

The message from HMRC is clear: there are fewer and fewer places to hide. However, this approach brings risks for the tax authority itself. Given the financial and emotional toll of tax enquiries, HMRC must ensure the information collated, such as social media posts, is used in a targeted and carefully considered way.

Investment in HMRC compliance activity – and potentially a more targeted approach – is to be welcomed. However, the key for HMRC is ensuring that the new officers are well-trained and that the information gathered is considered carefully and rigorously before opening potentially disruptive probes into high-profile taxpayers’ affairs.

Alistair Culverwell is head of tax dispute resolution at Forvis Mazars

While the after-work crowd deserts the pub, weekday evening padel bookings are heading skywards, says Playtomic’s Alan Douglas.

Every town has one. The pub with a quiz and darts, the one with the best pint but the table by the fire is always taken. For generations, the local has been where Brits go to socialise, unwind and set the world to rights.

It’s an institution. But pubs are, sadly, in trouble. The British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) says 295 pubs closed in the first nine months of 2026. That’s roughly 5,000 jobs, most held by under-25s.

This raises a question: where is everyone going to socialise now? From where I sit, a growing number of them are playing padel.

Playtomic is the community platform for padel, running approximately 85 per cent of UK padel bookings, so I see the stats in real time and one specific trend strikes me: weekday evenings are booming.

In the first nine months of 2026, players made nearly 600,000 weekday bookings between 6pm and 9pm. That is twice as many as in the whole of 2025. September was the busiest month yet, touching 80,000 evening bookings.

Driving this trend are 25- to 44-year-olds, accounting for 63 per cent of these slots. These are working people, finishing their day and looking to socialise with friends. Not long ago, that meant the pub; now, it can mean padel.

Social padel is winning over Britons

Not every booking is pints lost, but habits are shifting for younger Brits. They are health-conscious and a round is not cheap.

Padel gives people much of what the pub once did. It’s played in groups of four, it’s sociable and fun for all abilities, and everyone leaves happy. Think of it like this: for the price of a couple of drinks you can have an hour’s good fun with your friends, with added cardio.

Increasingly, padel clubs are working out that cafes and courts go hand in hand. I walk into many busy padel clubs on weekday nights and see happy, sweaty groups, still in their kit, discussing great shots, often with a beer in hand. The social aspects of padel, on and off the court, are part of the reason why Brits have fallen for this sport.

The stats back up my anecdotal conclusions. The 2026 Playtomic and PwC Global Padel Report shows that UK padel has grown 86 per cent year-on-year since 2021, with many courts at 85 per cent occupancy or more and about half of UK players saying they struggle to book at peak times. 

Our own stats show that, on average in 2026, 62,000 people per month played padel for the first time. Over 60 per cent of them played again within four weeks. 

So, what does all this mean for the pub? The stats and stories suggest that the after-work social crowd hasn’t disappeared. Their want for routine, community and familiar faces hasn’t evaporated. They have simply found new pastures.

I hope the pub will always be part of British life, and I hope it gets the support it needs because it is one of our greatest exports. But if you want to know where a lot of Brits go at 7pm on a Tuesday night, increasingly, the answer is a glass and metal box with a net across the middle, four laughing, sweaty friends and a tipple afterwards.

Alan Douglas is Regional Manager UK and Ireland for Playtomic.

I have always wanted to drive like The Stig, but not right here, not now. Twenty years ago, Ben Collins – the ‘tame racing driver’ behind the tinted visor – lost control of a Koenigsegg CCX on this very corner, crashing violently and expensively backwards through a tyre wall. The curve in question is the flat-out Follow Through, which slices across the centre of Dunsfold Aerodrome – better known as the Top Gear Test Track. I have already turned in, it’s too late to brake and I’m carrying way more speed than seems sensible. I feel the car go light and twitch slightly as it hits the destabilising hump near the apex, but try to ignore every instinct shouting at me to back off. Calmly, almost serenely, the Artura settles on its suspension, holds its line and accelerates away. Wow, that was fast. 

After Collins’ crash in 2006, Koenigsegg fitted the CCX with a new rear spoiler to boost downforce and stability. But as I push the McLaren to its limits – and a fraction beyond – around slower, less consequential corners such as Chicago, Hammerhead and Gambon, it’s clear this supercar is already well sorted. The Artura can make anyone drive like The Stig. Or feel as if they can, at least.

New era for McLaren Automotive

Like the Alpine A110 or just about any recent Aston Martin, the Artura is proof that critical acclaim doesn’t always translate into sales success. We gave the updated 2024 model a full five stars in our review, yet it remains a rarity, even by supercar standards. When did you last see one?

However, big changes are afoot in Woking, which has just received an investment of £500 million to create 1,000 jobs over the next six years, and develop a new range of cars – including the oh-so-inevitable SUV. There’s also a redesigned logo, a forthcoming new factory and the stunning McL 6GT concept, due to enter limited production in 2028.

All of which means McLaren’s current models are now living on borrowed time. The end of 750S production has already been marked by the special edition 788HS, while the GTS could be phased out in early 2027. The Artura likely won’t be far behind them. 

So, when an invitation arrived to revisit the Artura on UK roads, followed by a blast around the Top Gear Test Track, I jumped at the chance. Is McLaren’s ‘junior’ supercar really as good as I remembered?   

Petrol power with a hybrid punch

The day begins at the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC), where both the road car company and championship-winning Formula 1 team are based. Designed by Norman Foster, the glassy, clinically clean building resembles a space station that has landed in the Surrey countryside. For sheer wow-factor, no other car factory I have visited – including those in Maranello and Sant’Agata Bolognese – comes close. 

After a tour that takes in several McLaren F1s, classic race cars in various states of undress and the largest collection of motorsport trophies in the world, I’m introduced to Richard Jackson. “The Artura’s powertrain was born off the back of the Mclaren P1,” Jackson explains. “We wanted to prove that hybridisation is about more than just a Toyota Prius.” The 120-degree V6 has a low centre of gravity and is unusually compact, helping to save weight. “The engine is 40kg lighter than our V8, while the e-motor weighs just 15kg. Altogether, the hybrid hardware adds 80-100kg.”

The technology, since adapted for McLaren’s flagship £2 million W1, not only saves fuel, but allows the Artura to drive 21 miles in EV mode and – most importantly – gives it an almighty wallop of extra performance. “Engines are very important to us,” adds Jackson. “We talk a lot about the crescendo. You need to chase the revs to enjoy the car fully.” Duly noted.

The first part of my drive is a circuitous road route from the MTC to Dunsfold in the open-top Artura Spider. Its folding roof is made from carbon fibre composite and can disappear beneath the rear deck in 11 seconds. Alternatively, if the weather turns a bit ‘British’, you can simply lower the vertical rear window to turn up the V6 volume.  

The Spider’s carbon monocoque chassis makes it just as rigid as the coupe, which pays dividends on potholed rural roads that are, regrettably, also a bit British. I have to activate the hydraulic nose lift on the roughest sections of tarmac to avoid grinding the chin spoiler, but the Artura never feels jittery or discombobulated. It moves with deftness and precision, relaying messages to your fingers, feet and posterior with utter clarity. You feel hard-wired into the car, rather than like an adversary trying to tame it.    

As ever with McLarens, the hydraulic steering is a highlight. While its rivals all rely on electric assistance, Woking still does things the old-fashioned way – and the Artura is greater for it. Like any modern supercar, the Artura has more power than you can realistically deploy on the road – without getting locked up, at least. Yet the plug-in hybrid system also widens its breadth of abilities. 

Sometimes it’s nice to simply cruise in EV mode, for instance, enjoying the calm ride and crisp tactility in near-silence. The eager and ever-ready torque of the frisbee-sized electric motor also makes for safe and rapid overtakes when you aren’t minded to chase that high-rev crescendo. 

Equally, much as I love the (V8, non-hybrid) McLaren 750S, it’s quite a hardcore proposition for a motorway commute or popping to the shops. The Artura is more like a Porsche 911 Turbo: a supercar you could happily drive every day. Spec one in a subtle colour – i.e. not the signature Papaya orange – and it almost flies below the radar, helped by modest proportions and an absence of aero addenda. 

Taking it to the track

All that easygoing civility doesn’t mean the Artura can’t raise its game, though. Far from it. Some 700hp and 531lb ft of torque are force-fed to the rear wheels via a dual-clutch auto gearbox and electronic differential. Use launch control and you can blast to 62mph in 3.0 seconds. Maximum speed is 205mph. 

Arriving at Dunsfold, the track looks larger and more intimidating than on television. The wide tarmac makes picking the right line even more important, and there are places where the grass has been scuffed by skidding tyres. The Artura’s standard Club Sport seats move through an elliptical arc to keep you tightly ensconced, while the steering wheel is devoid of any buttons at all. We start with a few warm-up exercises on-track, including a launch control getaway. Yet the way the Artura takes off still elicits an involuntary “ooof”. Select launch mode, hold the brake with your left foot and then push your right sole to the floor. There’s no squirm from the chassis or scrabble from the rear Pirellis; the Artura simply grips and goes. 

Our next exercise uses the Variable Drift Control (VDC), which allows you to determine how much the car will slide before its stability system kicks in. The easiest way to test it is via a full-bore, tyre-smoking start while turning the front wheels – the ‘Ford Mustang exiting a car show’ manoeuvre, in other words. With VDC on, the Artura will execute a graceful slide, then gather itself up and blast away. With the software switched off, it’s a swift reminder of how 700hp can send you immediately and irretrievably sideways… 

The final warm-up is a slalom between white lines along the runway, switching between drive modes to experience the car’s behaviour. The adaptive dampers have notably more squish in Comfort mode, Sport feels exuberant and playful, while Track is ruthlessly focused on lap times. In all settings, however, the Artura’s modest inertia (kerb weight is 1,498kg for the coupe, 1,560kg for the Spider) and fundamental mid-engined balance shine through.

Time for a Top Gear power lap

Finally, it’s time to drive the circuit – thankfully without Jeremy Clarkson adding my name to the Power Lap leaderboard afterwards. Typically in such situations, your undivided attention is on the track itself, rather than on evaluating the car, but after a couple of laps – and a misspent youth watching golden era Top Gear – I’m pretty confident that I know where I’m going. 

As on the road, there’s a deep sense of connection between the car and driver. The Artura is on your side, fluid when you string a complex of corners together and forgiving when you don’t. It joins the dots around Dunsfold with athletic poise and expressive feedback, keeping it tight through Willson and Chicago, then sliding gleefully around Bacharach.

Electric ‘torque fill’ makes the car instantly responsive, but its engine also loves to rev, spinning towards its 8,500rpm limiter with reckless enthusiasm. Gearshifts are equally immediate, each new ratio banged home with a well-padded thump, plus occasional crackles from the twin tailpipes. Interestingly, the long, slender paddles behind the steering wheel operate on a rocker system, so you can pull or push on either side to shift up or down.

My only cause for complaint – and it’s a familiar one in Artura reviews – is that the engine could be more characterful. Like the hybridised V8 in a Lamborghini Temerario, McLaren’s V6 only really sounds exciting when you’re closing in on the redline. Perhaps in normal driving you will appreciate its civility, but I’d prefer Track mode to broaden the car’s vocal range. Still, it’s nothing that you couldn’t fix by bolting on an aftermarket exhaust.  

Verdict: McLaren Artura 2026

Priced from around £220,000, the McLaren occupies the middle ground between the much pricier Temerario and Ferrari 296 GTB and (relatively) more affordable supercars such as the 911 Turbo S, Aston Martin Vantage and Mercedes-AMG GT 63. 

Alternatively, you could find a three- or four-year-old Artura with less than 20,000 miles for around £125,000. In 2026, that is 911 Carrera S money – and it buys you a full-paid-up 700hp supercar. Makes you think doesn’t it?

The Artura has long felt overshadowed by McLaren’s faster and more visceral 750S, along with some of its showier, shoutier rivals from Italy. True, it takes a bit more time to appreciate its talents, but there’s a depth and maturity here that bodes well for McLaren’s next chapter. Whatever that may bring.

John Healey’s energy bills support package was meant to be targeted. But a City AM analysis has found homes worth millions are in line for a handout, while others in poorer areas will get nothing.

John Healey’s maiden fiscal event was nothing if not targeted. Painful tax rises – be they on banks or gambling firms – were “targeted” at industries the Chancellor deemed ripe for a raid.

The word “targeted” appeared as many as 30 times in the Budget document published to mark Healey’s big day, as officials sought to play down fiscal significance of their measures.

The biggest of those changes – a £2.4bn promise to bung £100 to households to help them with their higher energy bills – claimed to be focused on poorer households.

But a City AM analysis of council tax data revealed Healey’s reliance on the outdated property tax means his payment will land in the bank accounts of moneyed professionals and retirees in London and the South East. Meanwhile other, less affluent households from elsewhere will miss out.

Council tax bands have not been set nationwide since the early 1990s – meaning they often inaccurately represent current property prices. Some areas, such as in central and suburban London postcodes, have rocketed in value over the past 30 years – while homes in deindustrialised parts of the country have fallen in real terms.

That means million-pound homes in some of the swankiest London postcodes – including Notting Hill, leafy Twickenham and Primrose Hill – are in line for the energy handout, while homes in towns with much lower property prices, including Blackpool and Aberdeen, are not.

“Using 1991 house prices to target 2026 support was never going to be a good design,” Arun Advani, a director of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation (Centax), says. “After the support during Covid and the 2022 energy crisis, it is a sad indictment of government that a more effective way to target relief still hasn’t been created.”

The City AM analysis found freehold properties with as many as five bedrooms – in areas like Peckham, Nunhead and Camberwell – will receive the targeted support. The pocket of south east London was among the most deprived parts of the capital when the government evaluated council tax bands 35 years ago. Since then, however, the area has enjoyed an influx of upwardly mobile professionals looking to snap up affordable large terraced homes within a stone’s throw of central London. 

In the 25 years to 2019, Peckham property prices rose by over 1,000 per cent, according Land Registry data. That means even the owners of the area’s largest properties will receive £100 from the taxpayer. Take 130 Ivydale Road, a five-bedroom home sandwiched between the picturesque Nunhead cemetery and a sports ground. Sold last year for £1.26m, it boasts three bathrooms, a well-kempt hydrangea-filled patio garden and a palatial open-plan kitchen. It will also get £100 from the government by January. 

Cast the net beyond London, and even properties situated in the more salubrious enclaves of the Cotswolds are in line for the bung.

Situated just five miles away from the picturesque market town of Burford, The Haven is on the market for £1.3m. Its estate agent describes it as a “superb home” in the “highly sought-after and quintessentially rural village” of Filkins. It “perfectly marries period charm with modern elegance”, according to Oxford estate agent Penny & Sinclair, with “a generous entrance hall, utility, sitting room with feature fireplace and log burner”. But with the extra £100 for heating, its prospective owner might not need to stock up on as much firewood as feared.

City AM even found smaller flats and homes in parts of prime central London – including Notting Hill and St John’s Wood – that are included in the scheme. Several band-D houses on the picturesque, cobbled St Petersberg Mews are now worth an estimated £1.6m.

That means that had John Healey ploughed ahead with a rumoured plan to reduce the mansion tax threshold to £1.5m, those homes would have been liable to both the impending ‘council tax surcharge’, and the ‘targeted’ energy support package.

“A hundred pounds is nice, but the point is it’s extremely badly targeted,” Greg Thwaites, interim chief economist at the Resolution Foundation, told the think tank’s post-Budget press conference.

“There are lots of people doing ok, who can probably manage without that money – and probably need to manage without that money – if we’re going to support the people we need to support.”

The scheme’s poor targeting means there are also plenty of losers. Those tend to be focused in Britain’s former industrial heartlands. Places like Aberdeen, Nottingham and Merthyr Tydfil, whose economies were thriving in the early 1990s thanks to Britain’s steel, oil and mining industries.

A two-bed semi on Aberdeen’s Cranford Road, pictured above, falls in council tax band E – and thus misses out on the payment. That’s despite the property being worth 89 per cent less than the mews houses in Notting Hill and 86 per cent less than the Ivydale Road five-bed.

See also, the band-E, £250,000 home in Methyr Tydfil (below), the south Wales town once known as ‘the iron capital of the world’. Now, nearly 30 per cent of its residents are listed as economically inactive, as deindustrialisation and economic dislocation robbed it of high-skilled jobs and led its property prices to stagnate.

John Healey, for his part, has defended the scheme’s structure, hailing it as “real help” when people “need it most”. He will be glad, no doubt, to have the strident support of Martin Lewis, too. The all-powerful Money Saving Expert boss was fast out of the traps to declare it the “least worst option” for a package of this kind. “If you’re going to do an intervention, I think the mechanism of the intervention is right,” he said after visiting Downing Street ahead of the Budget.

A look at predicted energy prices at the start of next year and the reasons to intervene are obvious. Household bills are expected to jump some 27 per cent in early 2027 – roughly £300 for the average home.

But it is also those bleak forecasts that help explain why economists who have run the rule over the scheme and who it will benefit are in an altogether less celebratory mood than Healey and his money saving acolyte.

“It means a lot of cash going going to people that don’t need it,” Centax’s Advani says, “and some people who do need the support completely missing out.”
